cases.question: Why was March 2018 so bad for deliveries?
cases.headline: March 2018 was genuinely elevated for late deliveries: 19.0% of the 7,003 delivered orders were late versus a 5.8% baseline, a gap of 13.2 percentage points, and the pattern was systemic rather than confined to a few states or sellers.
notes: Late rate was 19.0% against a 5.8% baseline (delta 13.2 points), with 1,328 late orders out of 7,003 delivered.
The top driver was carrier_transit: transit averaged 12.97 days versus a 9.06-day baseline, roughly 3.9 days longer, while handling was only slightly above baseline (3.33 vs 3.19 days).
The problem was systemic: excluding the two worst states still left a 23.7% late rate, and late orders spanned 466 sellers with the top 5 accounting for only 11.5% of them.
It was concentrated geographically: RJ ran 34.5% late (baseline 10.5%, 208 excess late orders), MG 20.4% (baseline 3.3%, 147 excess), and SP 9.4% (baseline 4.1%, 158 excess).
Late deliveries coincided with much worse reviews: average 2.07 versus 4.21 for on-time, with a 59.3% one-star share versus 7.9%.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Some category samples are small, e.g. audio with only 33 orders, so its 42.4% rate is unstable.
Promised days were actually shorter than baseline (22.03 vs 23.78), so the elevated late rate is not explained by longer promises.

cases.question: What went wrong with deliveries in February 2018?
cases.headline: February 2018 was an unusually late month: 14.1% of delivered orders arrived late versus a 6.3% baseline, with the gap concentrated in carrier transit time.
notes: Late rate was 14.1% against a 6.3% baseline, a gap of 7.8 percentage points across 6,555 delivered orders (926 late).
Carrier transit averaged 13.38 days versus a 9.05-day baseline, about 4.3 days longer; handling time rose only modestly, from 3.18 to 3.56 days.
The pattern was systemic: excluding the two worst states, the late rate was still 14.3%, and late orders spanned 357 sellers, with the top five accounting for 13.9% of them.
RJ stood out with a 34.0% late rate versus a 10.5% baseline (207 excess late orders); SC was at 24.0% versus 7.0%, and SP at 7.3% versus 4.3%.
Late deliveries coincided with much lower review scores: 1.91 average versus 4.2 on time, and 64.1% one-star reviews versus 7.7%.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category and seller breakdowns are small in places (for example 53 orders for construction_tools_construction), so their rates are less reliable.
The findings describe associations only; they do not establish causes.

cases.question: Why were deliveries late in November 2017?
cases.headline: November 2017 was an unusually late month: 12.4% of delivered orders were late versus a 6.3% baseline, with the gap concentrated in carrier transit time and in RJ.
notes: Late rate was 12.4% (904 of 7,288 delivered orders) against a 6.3% baseline, a gap of 6.1 percentage points.
Carrier transit was the top driver: 11.09 days versus 9.2 days baseline, about 1.9 days longer; handling was 4.07 days versus 3.13 days, about 0.9 days longer.
The pattern was systemic rather than confined to a few states: the late rate excluding the top two states was still 13.0%.
RJ stood out with a 26.0% late rate versus 10.9% baseline (153 excess late orders); SP had 7.0% versus 4.3% (77 excess) and RS 12.7% versus 5.6% (29 excess).
Late orders coincided with much lower reviews: average 2.2 versus 4.24 for on-time orders, and 55.9% of late orders received one star versus 7.1% of on-time orders.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category samples are small (home_confort n=40, office_furniture n=75, books_general_interest n=37), so those rates are unstable.
Late orders were spread across 325 sellers, with the top five accounting for only 18.4% of them, so no single seller explains the period.
Promised delivery time was actually shorter than baseline (22.56 versus 23.74 days), so the late rate reflects actual delivery times rather than longer promises.

cases.question: Why were deliveries to Rio de Janeiro so late in March 2018?
cases.headline: Deliveries to Rio de Janeiro in March 2018 were unusually late: 34.5% of 864 orders arrived late versus a 10.5% baseline, and the gap was concentrated in carrier transit time.
notes: The late rate was 34.5% (298 of 864 orders), 24.0 percentage points above the 10.5% baseline.
Carrier transit averaged 21.08 days versus an 11.35-day baseline, about 9.7 days longer, while handling time was essentially flat (3.21 vs 3.28 days).
The promised window was slightly longer than baseline (27.95 vs 26.15 days), so the extra transit still exceeded the promise.
Late orders were spread across many sellers: 175 sellers had late orders, and the top five accounted for only 14.4% of them.
Late deliveries coincided with much lower review scores (1.67 vs 4.06 on time), and 72.6% of late-order reviews were one star versus 10.8% for on-time orders.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category rates rest on small samples (garden_tools n=32, watches_gifts n=59, bed_bath_table n=96), so those figures are noisy.
Review comparisons cover only orders with reviews (285 late, 563 on time) and reflect the reviewers, not all orders.

cases.question: Investigate late deliveries to Minas Gerais in March 2018.
cases.headline: Late deliveries to Minas Gerais in March 2018 were elevated: 20.4% of 856 delivered orders were late versus a 3.3% baseline, with the gap concentrated in carrier transit time.
notes: 175 of 856 delivered orders were late (20.4%), about 17.1 percentage points above the 3.3% baseline.
Transit took 13.19 days versus an 8.43-day baseline, roughly 4.8 days longer, while handling was only modestly higher (3.57 vs 3.18 days).
The promised window was actually shorter than baseline (22.49 vs 24.62 days), so the longer transit coincided with a tighter promise.

Late orders were spread across 118 sellers, with the top five accounting for 16.6% of them, and the highest late rates appeared in bed_bath_table (34.9%, n=83), health_beauty (27.8%, n=79) and housewares (26.8%, n=41).
Late orders coincided with lower review scores (2.15 vs 4.08 on time) and a much higher one-star share (58.3% vs 9.4%).
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category and seller figures are small samples (e.g., 41-83 orders per top category), so rates are noisy.
Review comparisons cover only orders with reviews (168 late, 679 on time).

cases.question: Why did late deliveries rise in December 2017?
cases.headline: December 2017 was not unusual overall: the late rate was 7.5% versus a 6.7% baseline, a gap of 0.8 points, and the playbook verdict is nothing_notable.
notes: Late deliveries were 411 of 5,513 delivered orders (7.5%), against a 6.7% baseline, a difference of 0.8 points.
The excess was concentrated in RJ: 746 orders at a 24.0% late rate versus an 11.4% baseline, about 94 excess late orders. Excluding RJ and RS, the late rate was 4.5%.
Handling averaged 3.72 days versus 3.17 baseline and transit 11.67 days versus 9.2 baseline, about 2.5 days longer; promised delivery windows were also longer (27.68 versus 23.4 days).
Late orders coincided with much lower review scores (2.11 versus 4.24) and a 58.4% one-star share versus 7.0% for on-time orders.
Small categories showed higher late rates (musical_instruments 19.5% on 41 orders, baby 14.1% on 135, office_furniture 13.2% on 38), but these samples are small.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Late orders were spread across 195 sellers, and the top 5 sellers account for only 17.3% of late orders, so no single seller explains the period.
Category-level rates rest on small order counts (38 to 135 orders).
The findings give no top driver (top_driver is none), so no single factor is identified.

cases.question: Why did review scores drop in March 2018?
cases.headline: March 2018 review scores were unusually low, averaging 3.75 versus a 4.11 baseline, with the one-star share nearly doubling to 19.0% from 10.9%.
notes: The drop was concentrated in late deliveries: 56.6% of one-star reviews came from late orders, and late delivery contributed 7.8 of the 8.1-point rise in one-star share.
On-time orders contributed only 0.3 points and not-delivered orders roughly zero, so the shift was not spread evenly across delivery outcomes.
Among categories, audio (2.94 vs 3.92 baseline, n=33), construction tools (3.36 vs 4.11, n=51), and toys (3.63 vs 4.19, n=221) scored lowest.
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Several category and seller samples are small (n=32 to n=51), so their scores are less stable.
Seller-level findings may reflect multi-seller attribution rather than a single seller's performance.

cases.question: What caused the low review scores in February 2018?
cases.headline: February 2018 review scores were below baseline, with late delivery the top associated driver.
notes: Average score was 3.83 versus a baseline of 4.11, and the one-star share was 17.1% versus 11.0% (a 6.1 point gap).
Late delivery was the top driver, contributing 5.7 of the 6.1 point one-star gap; on-time contributed 0.5 and not-delivered -0.1.
Among one-star reviews, 51.2% came from late orders, 37.9% from on-time orders, and 10.9% from not-delivered orders.
The weakest category by score was computers_accessories (3.45 vs 4.0 baseline, n=795), followed by luggage_accessories (3.5 vs 4.35, n=44) and food (3.67 vs 4.26, n=31).
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Some category and seller samples are small (e.g., luggage_accessories n=44, food n=31, sellers n=32-49), so their scores are less stable.
Seller-level findings may reflect multi-seller attribution rather than a single seller's performance.

cases.question: Why are customers in Rio de Janeiro giving low reviews in March 2018?
cases.headline: Reviews in Rio de Janeiro in March 2018 were unusually low, with an average score of 3.18 versus a 3.93 baseline and a one-star share of 33.5% versus 15.7%.
notes: The one-star share was 17.8 percentage points above baseline, and late delivery was the top driver.
Among one-star reviews, 69.7% came from late orders, 20.5% from on-time orders, and 9.8% from not-delivered orders.
Late delivery contributed 17.1 points to the one-star share, while on-time contributed 0.1 points and not-delivered 0.6 points.
The lowest-scoring categories were electronics (2.92 vs 3.86 baseline, n=45), sports_leisure (3.01 vs 3.91, n=77), and watches_gifts (2.95 vs 3.82, n=59).
No worst sellers were identified in the findings.
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Category samples are small (n=45 to 77), so those category-level scores are less reliable.
The findings do not attribute issues to individual sellers, so multi-seller effects cannot be separated.

cases.question: Why did review scores fall in November 2017?
cases.headline: November 2017 review scores were below baseline, with the drop concentrated in late deliveries.
notes: Average score was 3.91 versus a baseline of 4.10, and the one-star share was 15.1% versus 11.2%.
Late delivery was the top driver, contributing 3.4 points of the 3.9-point gap.
Among one-star reviews, 43.9% came from late orders, 39.9% from on-time orders, and 16.3% from not-delivered orders.
The lowest-scoring categories were home_confort (3.2 vs 3.9 baseline), fashion_bags_accessories (3.56 vs 4.21), and office_furniture (2.91 vs 3.54).
The lowest-scoring sellers had small samples: 43, 66, and 50 reviews, with scores of 2.37, 2.63, and 2.97.
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Some category and seller samples are small, and seller baselines are not available.
Seller-level results may reflect multi-seller attribution.

cases.question: Why were deliveries so bad in July 2017?
cases.headline: July 2017 was not an unusually bad delivery month: the late rate was 2.8%, well below the 7.0% baseline.
notes: The late rate of 2.8% was 4.2 percentage points below the 7.0% baseline, so the period was calmer than usual rather than worse.
Handling averaged 3.11 days versus a 3.21-day baseline, and transit averaged 8.51 days versus a 9.38-day baseline, about 0.9 days shorter.
The three states with the most late orders (SC, PR, RS) all came in below their baselines, and the rate excluding the top two states was also 2.8%.
Late orders were concentrated in a few categories: consoles_games at 11.1% versus a 5.9% baseline, luggage_accessories at 6.9% versus 4.1%, and fashion_bags_accessories at 6.2% versus 5.6%.
Late deliveries coincided with much lower review scores: 2.25 average for late orders versus 4.32 for on-time orders, and 54.3% of late orders got one star versus 5.5% of on-time orders.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Late orders were spread across 83 sellers, and the top five sellers accounted for only 19.4% of them, so no single seller explains the pattern.
Category samples are small (for example, 45 orders in consoles_games), so those rates are noisy.

cases.question: Investigate the late deliveries in June 2018.
cases.headline: June 2018 was not unusual for late deliveries: the late rate was 1.2%, well below the 7.2% baseline.
notes: Of 6,096 delivered orders, 71 were late, a 1.2% late rate versus a 7.2% baseline, about 6.0 points lower.
Handling averaged 2.57 days versus 3.25 days at baseline, and transit averaged 6.68 days versus 9.52 days at baseline, about 2.8 days shorter.
Promised delivery windows were longer than baseline, 27.77 days versus 23.37 days.
The states with the most late orders (GO, DF, ES) all had late rates below their baselines, and the rate excluding the top two states was also 1.2%.
Late orders coincided with lower review scores: 2.31 average versus 4.33 for on-time orders, and 52.1% one-star reviews versus 6.6%.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Late orders were spread across 58 sellers, and the top five sellers accounted for 16.9% of them, so no single seller stands out.
Category samples are small (for example, 30 drinks orders), which limits how much can be read into category-level rates.

cases.question: What went wrong with deliveries in May 2017?
cases.headline: May 2017 was not an unusually bad delivery month: the late rate was 3.0%, below the 6.9% baseline, so the premise of a delivery problem is not supported by the data.
notes: Late orders were 106 of 3,545 delivered orders, a 3.0% late rate versus a 6.9% baseline, about 3.9 points lower.
Handling averaged 2.98 days versus 3.21 baseline and transit 8.34 days versus 9.38 baseline, while promised delivery time was slightly longer at 24.28 days versus 23.62.
No state stood out for excess lateness: SP was 4.3% versus 4.5% baseline, SC 4.8% versus 8.4%, and PR 1.0% versus 4.2%; the rate excluding the top two states was 2.0%.
Late orders were spread across 80 sellers, and the top five sellers accounted for 16.0% of them; the highest listed seller rate was 7.0% against a 5.2% baseline, only about 1 excess late order.
Late deliveries coincided with much lower review scores: 2.74 average for late orders versus 4.28 on time, and 45.5% one-star reviews versus 6.3%.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Some category samples are small, for example home_confort with 32 orders and office_furniture with 42.
The review comparison covers 99 late and 3,418 on-time orders and is an association, not evidence of cause.

followups.question: Which 5 sellers had the most late orders?
followups.sql: WITH late_by_seller AS (SELECT oi.seller_id, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS late_orders FROM analytics.order_items AS oi JOIN analytics.orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE o.is_delivered AND o.is_late AND o.purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) GROUP BY oi.seller_id) SELECT seller_id, late_orders FROM late_by_seller ORDER BY late_orders DESC, seller_id LIMIT 5
followups.headline: The seller with the most late orders was 4869f7a5dfa277a7dca6462dcf3b52b2, with 35 late orders.

followups.question: How many late orders were there?
followups.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS late_orders FROM analytics.orders WHERE is_delivered AND is_late AND purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) AND customer_state = 'RJ' LIMIT 501
followups.headline: There were 298 late orders in the scope (orders purchased in March 2018, customer state RJ, delivered orders only).

followups.question: What was the average carrier transit time in days?
followups.sql: SELECT ROUND(CAST(AVG(carrier_transit_days) AS DECIMAL), 2) AS avg_carrier_transit_days FROM analytics.orders WHERE purchase_month = CAST('2018-02-01' AS DATE) AND is_delivered = TRUE AND carrier_transit_days IS NOT NULL LIMIT 501
followups.headline: The average carrier transit time was 13.38 days for delivered orders purchased in February 2018.

followups.question: How many orders were delivered?
followups.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders FROM analytics.orders WHERE is_delivered = TRUE AND purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) AND customer_state = 'MG' LIMIT 501
followups.headline: 856 orders were delivered for the March 2018 scope in Minas Gerais.

followups.question: What share of reviews were 1-star?
followups.sql: SELECT ROUND(CAST(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE review_score = 1) / COUNT(*) AS DECIMAL), 2) AS one_star_share_pct FROM analytics.orders WHERE purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) AND review_score IS NOT NULL LIMIT 501
followups.headline: About 19% of reviewed orders in March 2018 received a 1-star review.
